result.summary:
Gated docs/agents/test-specs/REQ-022.md (branch feature/WF02-REQ-022, commit 4a8119f) independently. Read core-directives.md, WF-02 Step 3b, docs/agents/design/REQ-022.md in full (all 5 ACs plus §0/§3/§4), handoffs/WF02-REQ-022/step-02c-security-reviewer.json in full, then the test spec file itself end to end -- not TEST-DESIGNER's result.summary.

Coverage check (per-AC, task step 2): every acceptance criterion (AC1-AC5) plus AC-security, AC-schema, AC-catalog has at least one verification case, each naming the exact route/command/callback pattern, exact fixture SQL, exact expected reply text, and an explicit Pass/FAIL condition. No 'TODO' found anywhere in the file (grepped). No case relies on subjective judgment ('check it looks right') -- every expected value is a literal string, a literal SQL predicate, or an exact count.

AC-security scrutinized in depth (task step 3), the central new case this spec adds over SECURITY-REVIEWER's flagged gap:
1. Fixture genuinely constructs an unrelated Attacker: two distinct users (tg_id 1000000510 Owner, 1000000511 Attacker) under one chapter -- same chapter is fine (chapter membership plays no role in decideWithdrawOutcome's ownership check, which compares registrations.user_id to actingUserId only). Attacker never registers for the event and has no registration row of their own; the attack is Attacker supplying the Owner's real registrationId directly to withdraw:confirm, exactly the forged-callback shape SECURITY-REVIEWER's handoff named. This is not a same-user/same-chapter false-positive risk -- the two users are genuinely independent rows with independent tg_ids resolved via resolveActingUser to independent users.id values.
2. Traced apps/bot/src/handlers/withdraw.ts and apps/bot/src/domain/registration.ts myself (not trusting the spec's or SECURITY-REVIEWER's claims). Confirmed directly in withdraw.ts lines 138-141 and 149-151: the 'not-owner' case and the 'not-found' case both reply with the exact same catalog.withdraw.refusedNotFound string -- this is the same source line's string constant reached from two different switch branches, not two independently-authored strings that merely happen to match today. Confirmed decideWithdrawOutcome (registration.ts:330-345) checks registrationExists (row 1) before ownerUserId (row 2), and withdrawRegistration (registration.ts:348-401) re-reads the target row fresh under FOR UPDATE by id alone (never trusting any earlier display-time read) and compares the row's actual userId column against the server-resolved actingUserId -- a mismatch returns {kind:'not-owner'} at line 334-336 before the UPDATE at line 387 is ever reached. This makes the spec's 'byte-identical reply' assertion a genuine non-disclosure proof, not a coincidence: both code paths that produce refusedNotFound are structurally the two ways of saying 'no row I can act on for you exists,' one for a truly nonexistent id and one for a real id owned by someone else, and they are provably the identical catalog reference.
3. Read the exact string values from apps/bot/src/i18n/en.ts lines 184-193 directly: usageNoId, confirmPrompt, confirmButton, cancelButton, confirmedReply, cancelledReply, refusedCheckedIn, refusedNotEligible, refusedNotFound all byte-match what AC1/AC-security/AC2/AC3 quote verbatim in the spec (e.g. refusedNotFound = "Registration not found.", confirmedReply = "You've withdrawn. Your seat has been freed.", refusedCheckedIn = "You've already checked in for this event -- attendance history can't be changed."). No drift between the spec's quoted expectations and the live source file.
4. Read-back assertions (task step 3's 'admission AND updated_at' requirement) are present exactly as required: AC-security captures the Owner's admission/updated_at/created_at as a 'before' snapshot, then asserts all three byte-identical after the forged attempt, plus a global audit_log count unchanged and zero registration.withdraw rows for that registration id specifically. This is a real state-unchanged proof, not merely 'admission still admitted.'

AC4 exact PK/created_at check (task step 6): verified the spec reads registrationIdBefore/createdAtBefore from a real SELECT immediately after the first real register callback (not assumed/computed), then asserts both are still exactly equal after a full register-withdraw-reregister cycle dispatched entirely through real callbacks, explicitly requiring millisecond-equality on created_at and a single-row count for the (event_id, user_id) pair. This matches the design's §3.1 claim (UPDATE's SET clause never names id or created_at) and is precise enough to catch a regression that reintroduced a plain INSERT.

AC2 freed-seat-is-genuinely-usable check (task step 7): verified as correctly designed -- capacity=2, two users fill the event (admitted count read as 2 via direct SQL, independent of the withdrawal), first user withdraws via the real confirm callback, admitted count re-read as 1 via a second independent SQL query (not inferred from a diff statement), then a third, previously-unregistered user registers via the real register callback and the spec asserts the reply starts with "You're in!" (admitted) rather than a waitlist reply -- this proves the freed seat is actually consumable by a new registrant end-to-end, not merely that a counter changed in isolation.

AC1 real dispatch check (task step 8): confirmed both the confirm and cancel paths are dispatched via bot.handleUpdate(callbackUpdate(...)) and bot.handleUpdate(messageUpdate(...)) against a real grammy Bot instance per the Shared Setup section (reusing the established REQ-020/REQ-021 harness shape) -- no mocked Context object anywhere in the spec; replies are read back from a real captured sendMessage array and DB state is read back via real psql/SQL queries against a real Postgres instance (docker compose). This is the same harness discipline already used and validated in REQ-020/REQ-021.

Failure-mode statement check (task step 9): every AC section (AC1, AC-security, AC2, AC3, AC4, AC5, AC-schema, AC-catalog) ends with an explicit 'Pass conditions' and a named FAIL condition describing exactly what a violation would look like -- none left implicit or deferred to TEST-RUNNER's judgment. The AC5 table additionally requires TEST-RUNNER to quote all four audit-count deltas explicitly, closing the risk of a report that says 'AC5 passed' without re-deriving it.

Cross-checked exact expected values against the real implementation (task step 4): en.ts string literals (above), the WITHDRAW_CONFIRM_PATTERN/WITHDRAW_CANCEL_PATTERN export names and index.ts registration lines the spec's AC-catalog grep expects, and decideWithdrawOutcome's row ordering all match the live source exactly -- no invented catalog key, no mismatched pattern name, no stale string.

No check failure found. PASS.
